title: Putting a season together
goal: Plan an amateur season around A, B and C races, with phases, recovery weeks and a taper, and say which parts rest on evidence and which on practice.

steps.title: Work backwards from the A race
steps.text:
Most coaches build an amateur season backwards from the main race:

| phase | rough length | main content |
|---|---|---|
| [transition](g:transition-phase) | 2–4 weeks after the last race | easy, unstructured |
| general preparation | 3–5 months | volume, mostly easy |
| specific preparation | 2–3 months | race-like intensity and duration |
| taper | about 2 weeks | volume cut, intensity kept |

Phase lengths are practice, not trial results. In skiers and biathletes who won Olympic or world gold, volume followed a traditional pattern, highest months before the peak, while the hours of hard training stayed about the same all year [[c:season-elite]]. Easy volume fell about 31% from general preparation to the peak.

claims.text: Gold-medal skiers' volume followed a traditional periodisation pattern, while the volume of hard training stayed stable across phases.

evidence.quote: Training volume and specificity distribution conformed to a traditional periodization model, but absolute volume of HIT remained stable across phases.
However, LIT training volume decreased by 31±17%

steps.title: A, B and C races
steps.text:
Few amateurs race only once. Coaches rank races ([A, B and C](g:priority-race)): this is **practice**, not tested in trials.

- **A**: 1–3 a season. Full taper, as in the last lesson.
- **B**: matter, but you train through most of the week and ease off for 2–3 days.
- **C**: training races. No easing; treat them as a hard session.

Elite skiers point the same way. With up to two race days a week for up to 14 weeks, they didn't follow the textbook taper [[c:season-mini-taper]]: they cut volume by only 4–15% in the last two weeks and did repeated short mini-tapers before races. Eleven athletes, observed, not tested, so it is weak evidence that a smaller cut can still work.

claims.text: Gold-medal skiers didn't follow the recommended taper; a busy race schedule calls for repeated mini-tapers.

evidence.quote: However, they did not follow suggested tapering practice derived from short-term experimental studies.
Rather than incorporating a single tapering phase, such a schedule may rather require the athlete to perform repeated “mini-tapers” prior to each competition.
With regards to training volume, we found only a 4 and 15% (NS) decrease in training volume during days -14 to -8 and days -7 to-1 respectively, compared to the pre-peaking phase.

steps.title: Recovery weeks and real life
steps.text:
A common pattern: 3 weeks of building, then a [recovery week](g:recovery-week) with about 30–50% less volume. It's everywhere in coaching but hasn't been tested against other ratios. Kiely's summary: beyond broad rules of thumb, there are no rules proven in trials [[c:season-no-rules]]. A small study in 32 amateur triathletes did find that two 4-week mesocycles and a 2-week taper raised performance without overreaching, in either order [[c:season-amateur]].

Life stress counts as load. Piled-up stress from work, family and poor sleep dampens adaptation and raises injury risk [[c:season-life-stress]]. So the recovery week is a default, to be moved: if your measures and feel say you're not absorbing training, ease off earlier.

claims.text: There are no empirically validated rules for detailed training planning, only broad guidelines.

evidence.quote: Beyond these broad rubrics, however, we have no empirically validated rules, and few specific guidelines.

claims.text: In amateur triathletes, two 4-week mesocycles followed by a 2-week taper improved performance without overreaching, whichever order was used.

evidence.quote: Independently of the periodization model, the combination of two four-week mesocycles followed by a two-week taper is an efficiency strategy to avoid overreaching, obtaining an increase in parasympathetic modulation.

claims.text: Accumulated stress from many sources dampens adaptation, lowers performance and raises injury risk.

evidence.quote: In summary, mounting evidence illustrates that excessively accumulating multi-source stress variously downregulates the immune system, motor coordination, cognition, mood, metabolism, and hormonal health; thereby dampening positive adaptation, diminishing athletic performance, elevating injury risk, and compromising recovery and recuperation

steps.title: Hours for a recovery week
steps.problem: A cyclist builds 8, 9 and 10 h over three weeks. She plans a recovery week with 40% less than her build-week average. How many hours?
steps: Keep one short harder session in it, so the week rests without going stale. The 40% is a habit of coaches, not a tested number.

steps.title: What's evidence and what's practice
steps.text:
Sort every piece of season advice by where it comes from:

| advice | basis |
|---|---|
| taper: volume −41–60%, intensity and frequency kept, about 2 weeks | **moderate**: two meta-analyses [[c:season-taper-recipe]] |
| HIIT blocks beat even spreading | **weak**: small, short trials |
| reverse order is better | **weak**: no advantage found |
| hard training kept all year, volume peaks early | **weak**: 11 elite athletes, observed |
| A/B/C races, mini-tapers | **practice** |
| 3:1 build:recovery weeks, transition phase | **practice**, untested |

Practice isn't wrong: it is what experienced coaches converged on. But hold it more loosely than the taper recipe, and let your own data correct it.

claims.text: The taper recipe is the best-supported part of season planning.

evidence.quote: A 2-wk taper during which training volume is exponentially reduced by 41-60% seems to be the most efficient strategy to maximize performance gains.
Current evidence suggests that a ≤21-day taper, in which training volume is progressively reduced by 41-60% without changing training intensity or frequency, is an effective tapering strategy.

points: Build the season backwards from the A race: transition, general preparation (volume), specific preparation (race-like work), taper.
Gold-medal skiers: volume highest months before the peak, hard training about stable all year (weak, observational).
A races get a full taper, B races a 2–3-day easing, C races none; busy calendars need mini-tapers (practice).
Recovery weeks (often 3:1) and phase lengths are practice, untested; life stress counts as load, so move them when needed.
Best evidence: the taper recipe (moderate). Block and reverse claims: weak. Everything else: practice.

variants.stem: In a typical amateur season plan, in what order do the phases come before the A race?

options.text: General preparation, specific preparation, taper
options.why: Right: broad volume first, race-like work next, then the cut-back.

options.text: Taper, general preparation, specific preparation
options.why: The taper comes last, just before the race.

options.text: Specific preparation, general preparation, taper
options.why: Race-specific work comes after the general base, not before.

options.text: Transition, taper, general preparation
options.why: The transition follows the last race; the taper sits right before the A race.

variants.stem: What is the transition phase for?

options.text: Recovering in body and mind after the season
options.why: Right: 2–4 weeks of easy, unstructured activity after the last race.

options.text: Building race-specific fitness
options.why: That's specific preparation, closer to the A race.

options.text: Clearing fatigue just before the A race
options.why: That's the taper.

options.text: Testing fitness at the start of the season
options.why: Testing can happen any time; it isn't what the transition is for.

variants.stem: In the year before their gold medals, elite skiers kept their hours of hard training about the same all year while easy volume fell by about 31% towards the peak. What does that suggest for an amateur cyclist?

options.text: Keep some hard work all year; let easy volume do the rising and falling
options.why: Right: hard training stayed steady; easy volume changed between phases.

options.text: Do no hard training until the last two months
options.why: The elites kept hard training throughout, not only near the peak.

options.text: Keep total volume the same all year
options.why: Volume did change: highest early, lower near the peak.

options.text: This proves traditional plans beat block plans
options.why: An observation of 11 athletes compares nothing; it can't prove one model better.

variants.stem: A cyclist's season: a club criterium every Tuesday, a regional road race in June, and a 735 km ride in August that is his main goal. How should he rank them?

options.text: August ride A, June race B, criteriums C
options.why: Right: one main goal gets the full taper; the June race a short easing; weekly races are training.

options.text: All of them A, with a full taper each
options.why: Tapering for weekly races would leave almost no real training.

options.text: Criteriums A, as he races them most often
options.why: How often you race doesn't make a race the goal.

options.text: June race A, August ride B
options.why: The August ride is his main goal, so it gets the A taper.

variants.stem: A triathlete has two A races only 3 weeks apart. What is the most sensible plan?

options.text: Full taper for the first, a few easy days, a short rebuild, a mini-taper
options.why: Right: there's no time for a full rebuild; keep fitness and freshen up again.

options.text: A full taper before each and no training in between
options.why: Weeks of reduced training in a row risk detraining.

options.text: Skip both tapers to keep fitness
options.why: Skipping tapers gives up the usual ~3% gain at both races.

options.text: A big overload block between the two races
options.why: Three weeks isn't enough to absorb an overload and taper again.

variants.stem: A triathlete builds 6, 7 and 8 h over three weeks and plans a recovery week 40% below the build average. How many hours is it?

options.why: Right: average 7 h; 7 × 0.60 = 4.2 h.
That's the 40% removed, not what's left.
That takes 40% off the last week (8 h), not the average.
That subtracts 0.4 h instead of 40%.

variants.stem: A runner builds 40, 45 and 50 km a week and plans a recovery week 30% below the build average. How many km?

options.why: Right: average 45 km; 45 × 0.70 = 31.5 km.

options.text: 35 km
options.why: That takes 30% off the last week (50 km), not the average.
That's the 30% removed, not what's left.

options.text: 15 km
options.why: That subtracts 30 km from the average.

variants.stem: A cyclist is in the second week of a 3-week build. Work is brutal, he sleeps 5 h a night, and his legs feel heavy on easy rides. What's the best call?

options.text: Bring the recovery week forward
options.why: Right: life stress counts as load; the 3:1 pattern is a default, not a rule.

options.text: Finish the build: the 3:1 pattern is proven
options.why: The 3:1 ratio is coaching practice, never tested in trials.

options.text: Add volume to make up for the missed adaptation
options.why: Extra load on top of heavy life stress raises the risk of poor adaptation.

options.text: Stop training for the rest of the month
options.why: A short easing is enough; weeks off would cost fitness.

variants.stem: Which piece of season advice rests on practice rather than trials?

options.text: Three build weeks, then one recovery week
options.why: Right: common in coaching, but never tested against other ratios.

options.text: Cut taper volume by about 41–60%
options.why: That comes from two meta-analyses.

options.text: Keep intensity during the taper
options.why: That's supported by the taper meta-analyses and reviews.

options.text: Taper for about 2 weeks
options.why: The 8–14-day window comes from meta-analyses.

variants.stem: A friend says: "Science proves block periodisation, 3:1 recovery weeks and tapering all work." Which part has the best evidence?

options.text: The taper
options.why: Right: two meta-analyses agree on the recipe (moderate).

options.text: Block periodisation
options.why: Small, short, low-quality trials: weak.

options.text: 3:1 recovery weeks
options.why: Practice only; no trials compared ratios.

options.text: They are equally well supported
options.why: They differ a lot: moderate, weak and untested.

variants.stem: A runner peaks at 70 km a week before her A marathon. Which taper fits the evidence best?

options.text: About 35 km a week for 2 weeks, keeping her short fast sessions
options.why: Right: a 50% volume cut, about 2 weeks, intensity and frequency kept.

options.text: About 65 km a week, cutting only the fast sessions
options.why: That cuts intensity, the part to keep, and barely touches volume.

options.text: About 35 km a week for 6 weeks, all easy
options.why: Six weeks is too long and dropping all fast running cuts intensity.

options.text: Complete rest for the last 10 days
options.why: Rest isn't a taper; it risks losing fitness and feeling flat.
